specPoints.text: know and use the relationship between average speed, distance moved and time taken: distance moved average speed = time taken

primer.text: Every journey has one number that sums it up: the average speed. You already met this relationship for steady motion; here it becomes the working tool for whole trips where the pace rises and falls. This lesson builds the equation, its units, and the triangle trick that rearranges it in seconds.

lessons.title: Average speed and the speed equation
lessons.opening: A trip rarely keeps one pace from start to finish, so physicists summarise it with a single value: the distance covered in each second of the whole journey. This lesson fixes the relationship among distance moved, time taken and average speed, and shows why that summary counts as a scalar.
keyPoints: Average speed is worked out from the whole trip: the full distance moved split by the full time taken.
Speed is a scalar quantity, so it states a magnitude only and never a direction.
Instantaneous pace can rise and fall during a journey, which is why the trip-wide average is the useful summary.
In standard units the relationship reads distance moved over time taken, giving metres per second (m/s).

low.restatement: To get an average speed, take the entire distance travelled and divide it by the entire time the trip lasted. The answer is a size only, never a direction.
low.analogy: It is like sharing a long car trip equally across every hour of the drive: some hours were fast, some slow, but the share per hour is one fair value.
low.examPointer: When a question names average speed, use the totals for the whole journey, not a value read from one short section of the trip.

medium.restatement: The defining relationship is average speed = distance moved / time taken, and because both inputs are totals, uneven pacing inside the journey does not matter.
medium.analogy: Think of a shopping bill: the total cost divided by the number of items gives one average price, however much individual items differed.
medium.examPointer: Scalar versus vector is a favourite one-mark question: speed has no direction attached, so any answer that mentions direction belongs to velocity instead.

check.stem: A jogger covers 1200 m of city streets in 480 s, having sped up and slowed down many times along the way. What average speed should be reported?

options.text: 1200 m divided by 480 s, the totals for the whole run
options.explanation: The trip-wide average uses the full distance and the full time, whatever the pacing in between.

options.text: The pace measured during the fastest street only
options.explanation: A single fastest segment describes one instant of the journey, not the trip-wide summary.

options.text: The mean of the fastest and slowest paces recorded
options.explanation: Averaging two extremes ignores how long each part of the journey lasted.

options.text: 480 s divided by 1200 m, to report seconds per metre
options.explanation: That inverts the relationship and yields s/m, not the m/s the quantity is defined with.

check.stem: Speed is classified as a scalar quantity. Which statement justifies that classification?

options.text: It has a magnitude but no direction attached
options.explanation: Scalars carry size only; direction is what would promote the quantity to a vector.

options.text: It can be measured with a stopwatch and a tape measure
options.explanation: How a quantity is measured says nothing about whether direction belongs to it.

options.text: It always takes positive values on a journey
options.explanation: Sign is not the test; a directed quantity could still stay positive while remaining a vector.

options.text: It changes when the object changes direction
options.explanation: A direction change leaves the pace itself untouched, which is exactly why speed ignores direction.

check.stem: A bus travels 300 m in 20 s, then crawls for 60 s before covering another 300 m in 20 s. Which value is its average speed across the whole trip?

options.text: 600 m over 100 s, which is 6.0 m/s
options.explanation: Total distance 600 m split by total time 100 s gives the trip-wide value of 6.0 m/s.

options.text: 15 m/s, the pace of the moving sections
options.explanation: 15 m/s describes only the two fast sections and ignores the 60 s of crawling.

options.text: 7.5 m/s, the mean of 15 m/s and 0 m/s
options.explanation: Averaging the two pace readings without weighting by their durations is not the defined relationship.

options.text: 5.0 m/s, because the crawl consumes most of the clock
options.explanation: No weighting rule sets the answer to 5.0 m/s; the totals give 6.0 m/s.

check.stem: In standard units, distance moved is in metres and time taken is in seconds. What unit therefore attaches to average speed?

options.text: metres per second (m/s)
options.explanation: Metres divided by seconds leaves m/s, the standard unit for this quantity.

options.text: seconds per metre (s/m)
options.explanation: That would follow from dividing time by distance, the reciprocal of the defined relationship.

options.text: metres times seconds (m·s)
options.explanation: Multiplying the units corresponds to multiplying the quantities, but the relationship divides them.

options.text: metres per second squared (m/s²)
options.explanation: Per second squared belongs to the rate of change of velocity, a different quantity met later in this topic.

check.stem: Two cyclists complete the same 40 km charity loop. One rides non-stop; the other stops for a long picnic and still finishes at the same clock time. What must be true?

options.text: Their average speeds across the loop are equal
options.explanation: Same distance in the same total time forces the same trip-wide value, however different the pacing was.

options.text: The picnicking cyclist travelled a shorter distance
options.explanation: The loop length is fixed at 40 km for both riders, so the distances match.

options.text: The non-stop cyclist must have ridden more slowly overall
options.explanation: Nothing forces a slower ride; the shared finish time pins the shared average.

options.text: Their instantaneous paces matched at every moment
options.explanation: Equal averages allow completely different pacing profiles; only the trip-wide summary is pinned.

check.stem: State, in words, how the average speed of a whole journey is calculated from its two totals.
check.modelAnswer: The average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time the journey took.

check.stem: Recall why the trip-wide value, rather than a single instantaneous reading, is normally quoted for a car journey.
check.modelAnswer: Because the pace of a real journey rises and falls, one instantaneous reading cannot represent it; the average sums the whole trip into a single fair value.

check.stem: Explain why two different hikers can finish the same trail in the same time while moving at different paces along the way.
check.modelAnswer: The average only fixes the ratio of total distance to total time. Two hikers with the same totals share that ratio, even if one strode fast in bursts and the other kept a slow steady rhythm, because the pacing profile is not part of the definition.

check.stem: A delivery drone travels 4.5 km across a city in 15 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
check.modelAnswer: Convert first: 4.5 km = 4500 m and 15 min = 900 s. The average speed is the distance moved divided by the time taken, so 4500 / 900 = 5.0 m/s.

lessons.title: Formula triangles and rearranging for distance and time
lessons.opening: The same relationship answers three different questions: how fast, how far, how long. Formula triangles turn that rearrangement into a cover-and-read trick. This lesson trains the trick and then proves each rearranged form against the original equation.
keyPoints: A formula triangle stores the relationship with the distance moved on top and speed and time taken sharing the base.
Covering the quantity you want leaves the layout of the other two: side by side means multiply, one above the other means divide.
Covering speed leaves distance over time; covering distance leaves speed and time side by side; covering time leaves distance over speed.
Keep the top-and-bottom order when reading a division: swapping numerator and denominator changes the answer.

low.restatement: Draw the triangle with distance on the top row and speed next to time on the bottom row. Hide one corner and the picture tells you the rearranged equation.
low.analogy: It works like a menu with one dish hidden: the remaining layout still tells you exactly how the visible items combine.
low.examPointer: Write the rearranged equation before substituting numbers; the layout alone earns no marks, the algebra does.

medium.restatement: The triangle is a picture of s = d / t: covering s shows d above t, covering t shows d beside s (multiply), and covering d shows s beside t (multiply).
medium.analogy: Treat the triangle as a rearrangement machine: one horizontal cover turns a division into a multiplication plus the remaining quotient.
medium.examPointer: Triangles are a memory aid, not a proof. If an examiner asks how the equation was rearranged, show the algebra: multiply both sides by time, then divide by speed as needed.

check.stem: On the formula triangle for this relationship, which corner must be covered to reveal distance moved = average speed × time taken?

options.text: The distance corner, leaving speed beside time
options.explanation: With the distance corner hidden, the two base corners sit side by side, which reads as a product.

options.text: The speed corner, leaving distance over time
options.explanation: Hiding speed reveals distance over time, which is the speed equation itself, not the distance form.

options.text: The time corner, leaving distance over speed
options.explanation: Hiding time gives the time form of the relationship, distance divided by speed.

options.text: Any corner, because every covering reveals the same equation
options.explanation: Each cover reveals a different rearrangement; the triangle has three distinct outputs.

check.stem: A learner covers the time corner and reads the triangle as time = speed ÷ distance. What went wrong?

options.text: The quotient was read upside down; the layout gives distance ÷ speed
options.explanation: With time covered, distance sits above speed, so the correct reading is distance divided by speed.

options.text: Nothing; time = speed ÷ distance is a valid form
options.explanation: That form is dimensionally wrong; seconds cannot come from (m/s) ÷ m.

options.text: The triangle should have been rotated first
options.explanation: Orientation is fixed by the stored relationship; rotation is not part of the method.

options.text: The learner should have covered two corners at once
options.explanation: Exactly one cover is made per rearrangement; covering two leaves nothing to read.

check.stem: Which rearranged form correctly solves the relationship for time taken?

options.text: time taken = distance moved ÷ average speed
options.explanation: Starting from s = d / t and multiplying both sides by t, then dividing by s, leaves t = d / s.

options.text: time taken = average speed ÷ distance moved
options.explanation: That quotient has units (m/s)/m = 1/s, which cannot be a time.

options.text: time taken = distance moved × average speed
options.explanation: Multiplying gives m × m/s = m²/s, not seconds.

options.text: time taken = average speed − distance moved
options.explanation: Subtraction mixes incompatible units and is not any rearrangement of the relationship.

check.stem: A plane holds a steady 250 m/s. Which rearrangement gives the distance it covers in a known time?

options.text: distance moved = average speed × time taken
options.explanation: With speed and time known, the product form returns the distance covered.

options.text: distance moved = average speed ÷ time taken
options.explanation: Dividing speed by time gives m/s per s, an acceleration-like unit, not a distance.

options.text: distance moved = time taken ÷ average speed
options.explanation: That quotient yields seconds per metre, not metres.

options.text: distance moved = 250 m/s regardless of the time
options.explanation: The constant 250 m/s is a pace, not a distance; the flight time must enter the calculation.

check.stem: Why can the triangle method be unsafe for equations beyond this topic's simple three-quantity relationships?

options.text: Triangles only encode one fixed multiply/divide layout, which not every equation has
options.explanation: Relationships with squares, sums or more terms cannot be captured by a single top-over-base picture.

options.text: Triangles stop working when the numbers get large
options.explanation: The size of the numbers is irrelevant; the structure of the equation is what matters.

options.text: Examiners deduct marks whenever a triangle is drawn
options.explanation: Credit follows the algebra; the triangle itself is just an aid, neither rewarded nor penalised.

options.text: Triangles only work for quantities measured in metres
options.explanation: The method is unit-blind; it depends on the equation's structure, not its units.

check.stem: State the two readings a formula triangle supports when the base corners sit side by side.
check.modelAnswer: Side-by-side corners read as a product: the covered quantity equals the product of the two visible ones.

check.stem: Recall the rearranged form a triangle gives when the distance corner is covered in the average-speed relationship.
check.modelAnswer: Covering distance leaves speed and time side by side, so distance moved = average speed × time taken.

check.stem: Explain why keeping the top-and-bottom order matters when a triangle shows one quantity above another.
check.modelAnswer: The vertical layout encodes a division, and division is not symmetric: distance over speed gives a time in seconds, while speed over distance would give seconds per metre, a meaningless quantity here. Swapping the levels therefore changes both the number and the unit of the answer.

check.stem: A bird holds a cruising pace of 4.5 m/s for 40 s across a field. Use the product form to calculate the distance it covers.
check.modelAnswer: Distance moved = average speed × time taken = 4.5 × 40 = 180 m.

glossary.definition: The single trip-wide value: the total distance moved divided by the total time taken.
A quantity that carries a magnitude only, with no direction attached; speed is one.
A cover-and-read memory aid: hiding one corner reveals whether the other two multiply or divide.
The standard unit of speed, written m/s, from metres divided by seconds.

workedExample.prompt: Planes cruise at a typical average speed of 250 m/s. Calculate the distance travelled by a plane holding this pace for 2 hours.
steps: List the known quantities: average speed = 250 m/s; time taken = 2 hours.
Convert the time into standard units: 2 hours = 2 × 60 × 60 = 7200 s.
Rearrange the relationship for distance: distance moved = average speed × time taken.
